claims.text: AgInSnPbBiTe5 is a high-entropy, CsCl-type metal-telluride superconductor with configurational mixing at the M site.
AgInSnPbBiTe5 has a robust superconducting state under ambient conditions.
High configurational entropy creates a uniformly disordered electronic and lattice environment.
The disordered environment stabilizes electron-phonon coupling against pressure.
High configurational entropy governs superconducting behavior by keeping Tc nearly invariant under pressure.
AgInSnPbBiTe5 has an almost pressure-independent Tc from approximately 13 to 35 GPa.
PbTe exhibits decreasing Tc as pressure increases.
AgPbBiTe3 exhibits a more pronounced pressure-induced decrease in Tc than AgInSnPbBiTe5.
When the compared tellurides have the CsCl-type structure, they are superconducting under high pressure.
Atomic-scale disorder averages out site-to-site variations in local electron-phonon coupling.
Averaging local coupling variations reduces the pressure sensitivity of electron-phonon coupling and preserves Tc.
The absence of extensive configurational disorder in PbTe or AgPbBiTe3 causes greater pressure sensitivity of electron-phonon coupling and Tc.
Configurational entropy at the M site is linked to the pressure robustness of superconductivity in MTe.
The proposed relationship applies to uniformly disordered superconductors containing five or more mixed elements at 5–35 at% each.
The relationship may fail when significant secondary phases form.
The relationship may fail or be obscured when a non-electron-phonon pairing mechanism dominates.
A comparison in which the HEA has Tc pressure dependence similar to or stronger than the baseline would falsify the proposed entropy-based pressure robustness.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that only configurational disorder differs, but replacing AgInSnPbBiTe5 with PbTe or AgPbBiTe3 also changes elemental identity, stoichiometry, electronic structure, and potentially phonon properties.
The design says to maintain constant temperature while the specified Tc measurements require temperature-dependent resistivity or susceptibility scans.
